blocks.text: At resonance the amplitude of an oscillator becomes very large. Both the amplitude and the sharpness of the resonance depend on the damping: the smaller the damping, the greater the amplitude and the sharper the resonance. A heavily damped system has a fairly flat resonance curve on an amplitude-frequency graph (Fig 14.20).

The effect of damping can be seen by hanging, from one rod, a pendulum with a light bob such as a pith ball and another of the same length with a heavy lead bob of equal size, and driving them with a third pendulum of the same length. The amplitude of the lead bob becomes much greater than that of the pith ball, because air resistance damps the light pith ball much more than the heavy lead bob.

blocks.alt: Amplitude against driving frequency, with the resonant frequency marked on the axis. Three curves peak there: light damping gives a tall, sharp peak, moderate damping a lower peak and heavy damping an almost flat curve.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.20: Damping system illustration (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.20).

blocks.title: Point to ponder: the Tacoma Narrows Bridge
blocks.text: Resonance matters in the design of bridges and other structures. The Tacoma Narrows Bridge (Washington, USA) opened in July 1940; four months later a moderate wind set it into large oscillations, and within hours part of the bridge broke and fell into the water.
Applications of resonance and standing waves
Many devices generate and use standing waves, and the link between standing waves and resonance can be studied with the Rubens tube, Chladni plates and acoustic levitation.

items: Rubens tube (Fig 14.21): a long metal pipe with a row of holes along its top, sealed at both ends; one end has a small loudspeaker driven by a frequency generator and the other is connected to a supply of flammable gas. Gas escaping from the holes is lit. At a resonant frequency a standing wave forms in the tube; more gas escapes where the pressure varies most, so the flames are higher there and lower at the nodes, revealing the standing wave.

blocks.alt: A gas cylinder feeds a long metal pipe with holes on top. The far end is closed by a membrane with a loudspeaker beyond it. A standing wave is drawn inside the pipe, and the flames above it are tall at the antinodes and short at the nodes.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.21: Rubens tube apparatus (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.21).

items: Chladni plate (Fig 14.22): a square or circular metal plate fixed at its centre to a vibrator. At the frequency of a resonant mode, nodes and antinodes form over the plate. Sand sprinkled on the plate is shaken away from the antinodes and collects along the nodal lines, which do not move, showing the pattern.

blocks.alt: (a) Classical Chladni plate: a flat square plate on a central support, held at one edge and bowed with a violin bow at the other while sand falls from a sand shaker; the sand lies along a grid of nodal lines. (b) Modern Chladni plate: the flat plate sits on a mechanical oscillator fed by an electrical signal input, with sand from a shaker forming rings.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.22: Chladni plates, (a) classical and (b) modern (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.22).

items: Acoustic levitation (Fig 14.23): high-frequency (ultrasonic) sound from a transducer is reflected by a reflector, and the incident and reflected waves form a standing wave. Small particles such as bits of styrofoam or droplets of water are held against gravity at the pressure nodes, which act as acoustic traps.

blocks.alt: An acoustic levitator: an ultrasonic transducer with a concave horn on a base, wired to a controller, and a reflector held above it on a stand. A floating droplet hangs between them. An enlarged view shows the standing wave between reflector and horn, the droplet held at a node and one wavelength lambda marked.
blocks.caption: Figure 14.23: Acoustic levitation setup (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 14.23).

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: The Rubens tube, also called a standing-wave flame tube, was invented by the German physicist Heinrich Rubens in 1905. Chladni plates were invented by the physicist and musical-instrument maker Ernst Chladni (1756-1827) in the late 18th century to show the complex patterns of standing-wave vibrations.
